title: World War Two, the “No Good” War
author: James Bovard
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/Bundesarchiv_Bild_146-1994-041-07_Dresden_zerstortes_Stadtzentrum-680x448.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/09/04/world-
war-two-the-no-good-war/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/Bundesarchiv_Bild_146-1994-041-07_Dresden_zerstortes_Stadtzentrum-680x448.jpg)

The ruins of Dresden, after the Allied bombing. Public domain.

September 1 is the anniversary of the start of World War Two in Europe. On
that date in 1939, Nazi Germany launched an invasion of Poland from the west
and a few weeks later, the Soviet Union invaded from the east. Hitler and
Stalin signed a Non-Aggression Pact shortly before they carved up Poland but
that ceasefire didn’t last beyond June 1941.

World War Two has been heralded for more than 50 years as the “Good War” – in
contrast to subsequent U.S. military debacles in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan,
Iraq, and Iran. But World War Two cannot be glorified without hiding a heap of
lies and millions of corpses.

Less than six months before the war started in Europe, H.L. Mencken warned in
the Baltimore Sun: “The main reason why it is easy to sell war to peaceful
people is that the demagogues who act as salesmen quickly acquire a monopoly
of both public information and public instruction.” Looking at the peril of
another world war, Mencken predicted, “On the day war is declared, the
Espionage Act will come into effect, and all free discussion will cease… Any
argument against the war itself, and any criticism of the persons appointed to
carry it on, will become aid and comfort to the enemy.” Mencken wrote, “A few
weeks of [pro-war] razzle-dazzle will suffice to convert most people to the
war and to intimidate and silence the stray recalcitrant who holds out.”
Thanks to massive pressure to conform and submit, “The dissenter is not only
suspected by all his neighbors; he also begins to suspect himself.”
Unfortunately, the U.S. government vindicated Mencken’s worst fears on
censorship during the war and far beyond.

President Franklin Roosevelt worked ceaselessly and shamelessly to drag
America into the European conflict. He capped off his 1940 reelection campaign
by promising voters: “[Your president says this country is not going to
war.](https://books.google.com/books?id=xTKvo-
cXv3EC&pg=PA250&lpg=PA250&dq=franklin+roosevelt+%22Your+president+says+this+country+is+not+going+to+war.%E2%80%9D&source=bl&ots=HPl3C-MJAx&sig=0dF3Hudv8h0a8QrQBBHCmkbrf88&hl=en&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwimgZ7-lcjeAhWK1VkKHTlfDN8Q6AEwBHoECAQQAQ#v=onepage&q=franklin%20roosevelt%20%22Your%20president%20says%20this%20country%20is%20not%20going%20to%20war.%E2%80%9D&f=false)”
FDR portrayed World War Two as a fight for democracy, which required endless
hornswoggling of the American public regarding U.S. allies.

The Roosevelt administration engineered a movie tribute to Stalin — _Mission
to Moscow_ — that was so slavish that Russian composer Dimitri Shostakovich
observed that “no Soviet propaganda agency would dare to present such
outrageous lies.” In his 1944 State of the Union address, Roosevelt denounced
those Americans with “such suspicious souls — who feared that I have made
‘commitments’ for the future which might pledge this Nation to secret
treaties” with Stalin at the summit of Allied leaders in Tehran the previous
month. Roosevelt helped set the two-tier attack that permeated much of postwar
American foreign policy — denouncing cynics, while betraying foreigners whom
the U.S. government pretended to champion.

In a private conversation at the Yalta conference in early 1945, Roosevelt
assured Stalin that he was feeling “more bloodthirsty” than when they
previously met. Immediately after the Yalta conference, the British and
American air forces turned Dresden into an inferno, killing up to 50,000
civilians. The Associated Press reported that “Allied air bosses” had adopted
“deliberate terror bombing of great German population centers as a ruthless
expedient to hasten Hitler’s doom.” Ravaging Dresden was intended to “‘add
immeasurably’ to Roosevelt’s strength in negotiating with the Russians at the
postwar peace table,” as Thomas Fleming noted in _The New Dealers’ War._ Vast
numbers of dead women and children became simply one more poker chip. Shortly
after the residents of Dresden were obliterated, Roosevelt pompously
announced, “I know that there is not room enough on Earth for both German
militarism and Christian decency.” Government censorship and intimidation
helped minimize critical coverage of the civilian carnage resulting from U.S.
carpet-bombing of cities in both Germany and Japan.

Prior to the Yalta conference, Roosevelt confided to the U.S. ambassador to
Russia that he believed that if he gave Stalin “everything I possibly can and
ask for nothing in return, noblesse oblige, he won’t try to annex anything and
will work with me for a world of democracy and peace.” Stalin wanted
assurances from Roosevelt and Churchill that millions of Soviet citizens who
had been captured during the war by the Germans or who had abandoned the
Soviet Union would be forcibly returned. After the war ended, Operation
Keelhaul forcibly sent two million Soviets to certain death or long-term
imprisonment in Siberia or elsewhere. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn called Operation
Keelhaul “the last secret” of World War II and it was covered up or ignored by
Western media until the 1970s. Those mass deaths facilitated by the U.S. and
British governments rarely rate even an asterisk by the media-beloved
historians who tout the “Good War.”

Many American soldiers and sailors died because of FDR’s boundless hatred of
Germans. In the final years of the war, FDR gave a huge boost to Nazi
propaganda when he floated plans to subjugate the German people permanently by
banning all factories and even airplanes in the conquered territory. The
president told Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau Jr., “We either have to
castrate the German people or you have to go to treat them in such manner so
they can’t just go on reproducing people who want to continue the way they
have in the past.” FDR declared that after the war, every German “should be
fed three times a day with…Army soup,” adding that “they will remember that
experience all their lives.” Cordell Hull, Roosevelt’s long-serving Secretary
of State, condemned the Morgenthau plan (as it became known) as an “extreme
starvation plan.” (David Beito’s book, [_FDR: A New Political
Life_](https://www.amazon.com/exec/obidos/ASIN/1637700695/reasonmagazinea-20/)
_,_ is an excellent source on FDR’s conniving.) The combination of the
Morgenthau Plan and the bombing of civilian areas in Dresden, Hamburg, and
other German cities, killing nearly 600,000 civilians, may have spurred far
more Germans to keep fighting to the death.

In the final communiqué from Yalta, Roosevelt, along with Churchill and
Stalin, declared that “a new situation has been created in Poland as a result
of her complete liberation by the Red Army.” Liberation? Tell that to the
Marines. A few weeks later, on March 1, 1945, FDR gave a speech to Congress
touting his triumph at Yalta, declaring, “The decision with respect to the
boundaries of Poland was, frankly, a compromise…. It will include, in the new,
strong Poland, quite a large slice of what now is called Germany.” He agreed
with Stalin at Yalta on moving the border of the Soviet Union far to the west
— thereby effectively conscripting 11 million Poles as new Soviet Union
citizens.

Roosevelt told Congress that the deal at Yalta was “the most hopeful agreement
possible for a free, independent, and prosperous Polish people.” But he
betrayed the exiled Polish government in London and signed off on Soviet-style
elections with no international observers — effectively giving Stalin
unlimited sway on choosing Poland’s rulers. Any illusions about Soviet
benevolence towards Poland should have been banished when the Red Army
massacred the Polish officer corps at Katyn Forest — an atrocity that the U.S.
government assiduously covered up (and blamed on the Nazis) during the war and
long after.

Poland was “compensated” for the loss of territory to the Soviet Union with a
huge swath of Germany, a simple cartographic revision that spurred vast human
carnage. But post-war atrocities against Germans were almost totally ignored
for the remainder of the twentieth century. In 2012, historian R. M. Douglas,
author of Orderly and Humane: The Expulsion of the Germans After the Second
World War (Yale University Press), [vividly
captured](https://www.chronicle.com/article/the-european-atrocity-you-never-
heard-about/#disqus_thread) the carnage that continued after the war formally
ended:

Between 1945 and 1950, Europe witnessed the largest episode of forced
migration, and perhaps the single greatest movement of population, in human
history. Between 12 million and 14 million German-speaking civilians -the
overwhelming majority of whom were women, old people, and children under 16
-”were forcibly ejected from their places of birth in Czechoslovakia, Hungary,
Romania, Yugoslavia, and what are today the western districts of Poland. As
The New York Times noted in December 1945, the number of people the Allies
proposed to transfer in just a few months was about the same as the total
number of all the immigrants admitted to the United States since the beginning
of the 20th century. They were deposited among the ruins of Allied-occupied
Germany to fend for themselves as best they could. The number who died as a
result of starvation, disease, beatings, or outright execution is unknown, but
conservative estimates suggest that at least 500,000 people lost their lives
in the course of the operation.

Most disturbingly of all, tens of thousands perished as a result of ill
treatment while being used as slave labor (or, in the Allies’ cynical
formulation, “reparations in kind”) in a vast network of camps extending
across central and southeastern Europe – many of which, like Auschwitz I and
Theresienstadt, were former German concentration camps kept in operation for
years after the war. Ironically, no more than 100 or so miles away from the
camps being put to this new use, the surviving Nazi leaders were being tried
by the Allies in the courtroom at Nuremberg on a bill of indictment that
listed “deportation and other inhumane acts committed against any civilian
population” under the heading of “crimes against humanity.”

By any measure, the postwar expulsions were a manmade disaster and one of the
most significant examples of the mass violation of human rights in recent
history. Yet although they occurred within living memory, in time of peace,
and in the middle of the world’s most densely populated continent, they remain
all but unknown outside Germany itself.

George Orwell denounced the “relocation” as an “enormous crime” that was
“[equivalent to transplanting the entire population of
Australia](https://newrepublic.com/article/102925/orderly-humane-expulsion-
germans-richard-evans).” Philosopher Bertrand Russell protested: “Are [mass
deportations crimes when
committed](https://books.google.com/books?id=3TfJcZMS6TIC&pg=PA162&lpg=PA162&dq=bertrand+russell+mass+deportations+crimes+when+committed+by+our+enemies+during+war+and+justifiable+measures+of+social+adjustment+when&source=bl&ots=-dhUYsg99y&sig=ACfU3U2Vq0854Ofx4iSNmRVZsn6GzK4JLQ&hl=en&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjb6oOI-
tHnAhWrSt8KHUmYDmwQ6AEwAXoECAkQAQ#v=onepage&q=bertrand%20russell%20mass%20deportations%20crimes%20when%20committed%20by%20our%20enemies%20during%20war%20and%20justifiable%20measures%20of%20social%20adjustment%20when&f=false)
by our enemies during war and justifiable measures of social adjustment when
carried out by our allies in time of peace?” But the German civilians killed
after the war were simply another asterisk ignored by Good War chroniclers.

Jon Utley was a legendary conservative-libertarian philanthropist who rescued
The American Conservative and also generously supported Antiwar.com. Utley’s
mother, Frida Utley, did piercing writing on the post-World War Two abuses in
Germany. Her pathbreaking work is archived [**here**.
](http://www.fredautley.com/) She wrote, “Some twelve million people were
expropriated and driven from their homes for no other crime than that of being
Germans. Out of a total of twelve to thirteen million people who had committed
the crime of belonging to the German race, four or five million are
unaccounted for. More people have been rendered homeless by an Allied peace
than by a Nazi war.”

Nazi Germany committed great crimes against humanity and that regime deserved
to be terminated by its opponents and its victims. But humanity was ill-served
when the victors were permitted to expunge all of their own atrocities and
lies. Legendary war correspondent Ernie Pyle offered a far more honest
assessment of World War Two than did FDR: “The war gets so complicated and
confused in my mind; on especially sad days, it’s almost impossible to believe
that anything is worth such mass slaughter and misery.” The halo that
kowtowing historians slapped over World War Two made it far easier ever since
for politicians to drag America into military quagmires.
